questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: In a web crawler, what does the crawl frontier contain?
options: Pages that have been fetched and are waiting for parsing and link extraction
Hosts that are temporarily excluded from fetching until their politeness delay elapses
URLs that have been discovered but not yet fetched, ordered for future fetching
Links between already-crawled pages, kept for later link-graph analysis and scoring

questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: Why do large crawlers use per-host back queues (Mercator style) instead of a single global priority queue?
options: So per-host rate limits can be enforced while workers stay busy on other hosts
So the crawler can guarantee a strict breadth-first traversal of the web graph
So duplicate URLs can be removed without running a separate URL-seen test
So the highest-priority pages are always fetched before any lower-priority page

questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: Your crawler uses a single FIFO queue. Shortly after starting from a few seed sites, most worker threads sit idle while a few hosts receive request bursts. What explains this?
options: The URL-seen test is silently discarding most newly extracted links before queueing
Extracted links mostly stay on the same host, so politeness delays serialize the queue
The frontier has exhausted its discovered URLs and is waiting on a new seed injection batch
DNS resolution is caching failures, so most hosts appear unreachable to the workers

questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: You must crawl a 500,000-page site under a politeness delay of 5 seconds between requests to that host. Roughly how long does the full crawl take, no matter how many workers you add?
options: About 8 hours
About 3 days
About 9 days
About 29 days

questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: You rank frontier URLs by a value score and always pop the maximum. Weeks in, entire mid-tier sites discovered early have never been visited. What design change addresses this best?
options: Reset all priority scores to zero weekly so every URL gets an equal chance eventually
Select among priority queues with probability weighted by priority instead of max-first
Raise the per-host politeness delay so high-priority hosts consume budget more slowly
Move the URL-seen test after the fetch stage so rediscovered URLs re-enter the frontier

questions.topic: The Crawl Frontier: Prioritization and Queue Management
questions.question: You are building a scoped research corpus of about 20 million pages from a few thousand approved hosts. Which frontier design is the most defensible starting point?
options: Per-host FIFO queues under a simple host-level scheduler, without multi-tier machinery
A full Mercator design with hundreds of front queues, since host fairness demands both tiers
A single global max-priority heap, since host fairness is irrelevant at this scale
A random-order frontier, since prioritization only matters beyond one billion pages

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: A crawler wants to check crawl permissions for `https://example.com/docs/page`. Where must it look?
options: `https://example.com/docs/robots.txt`, the robots file nearest the requested path
The `<meta name="robots">` tag on the page itself, fetched before crawling
`https://example.com/sitemap.xml`, which lists the crawlable URL inventory
`https://example.com/robots.txt`, the single file at the root of that origin

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: A robots.txt contains `Disallow: /search` and `Allow: /search/about` for your user agent. How should your crawler treat `https://site.com/search/about`?
options: Disallowed, because any matching Disallow rule always overrides an Allow rule
Disallowed, because rules apply in file order and the Disallow line appears first
Allowed, because the most specific rule, judged by longest path match, wins
Allowed, because Allow rules always override Disallow rules regardless of paths

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: Your fetch of a host's robots.txt returns HTTP 503 repeatedly. What is the conservative, standards-aligned behavior?
options: Treat the whole host as disallowed for now and retry the robots.txt fetch later
Treat the whole host as allowed, since only a parseable file can restrict crawling
Fall back to crawling only the homepage until the file becomes available again
Switch to a different user-agent string, since 503 usually signals an agent block

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: Mid-crawl, a host's median response time rises from 200 ms to 2 s and it begins returning 429 responses with `Retry-After: 120`. What should a well-behaved crawler do?
options: Keep the current rate but rotate alternate IPs so no single address exceeds limits
Pause that host for at least 120 seconds and resume with a longer inter-request delay
Drop the host from the frontier permanently, since a 429 response signals a hard crawl ban
Retry immediately at lower priority, since 429 responses are advisory, not binding

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: A source critical to your corpus sets `Crawl-delay: 60`, making its 2 million pages take years to fetch. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Honor the delay for HTML pages but fetch the bulk of the site with a headless browser
Ignore the directive, since Crawl-delay is nonstandard and absent from RFC 9309
Seek a sanctioned bulk channel, such as an API or data dump, or contact the operator
Spread requests across many worker IP addresses so each one honors the delay alone

questions.topic: Politeness: Rate Limits, robots.txt, and Crawl Delay
questions.question: Your crawler politely rate-limits per hostname, yet a small hosting provider complains you are overloading their server. What did the design miss?
options: The robots.txt cache expired, so each fetch re-downloaded the file and doubled load
The crawler ignored `Crawl-delay`, which shared hosting providers rely on exclusively
HTTP keep-alive was disabled, so connection setup costs multiplied the server load
Many distinct hostnames resolve to one server, so limits must also apply per IP

questions.question: Which situation is a crawler trap?
options: A calendar widget whose next-month link generates an unbounded series of unique URLs
A robots.txt file that disallows every path on the host for all user agents
A page whose outlinks all point to hosts that lie outside the configured crawl scope
A server that returns 429 responses whenever the crawler exceeds its rate limit

questions.question: Which URL normalization can be applied to any URL without risking a change in what the server returns?
options: Stripping every query parameter, since parameters only carry tracking information
Lowercasing the entire URL, including the path, so all aliases hash identically
Lowercasing the scheme and host and removing a default port like `:443` on HTTPS
Removing a trailing slash from the path, since directories and files are equivalent

questions.question: Your seen-URL test is passing, yet the crawl fetches the same article dozens of times under URLs differing only in `utm_source` values. What is the right fix?
options: Increase the per-host page budget so duplicates no longer crowd out fresh URLs
Strip known tracking parameters during canonicalization before the seen test runs
Fingerprint each fetched page's content and drop the request when the hash repeats
Lower the URL length cap so long campaign-tagged URLs are kept out of the frontier

questions.question: On an e-commerce host, crawled URLs grow into the millions while newly seen distinct content flattens out. Which frontier-side defense targets this pattern?
options: Refetching robots.txt more often, since the site likely added new Disallow rules
Switching from priority order to FIFO order so deep facet pages drain more quickly
Raising worker concurrency on that host so the URL backlog clears more quickly
Capping query-parameter counts and per-host budgets when content-per-URL collapses

questions.question: After adding aggressive query-parameter stripping, coverage of a forum's long discussion threads silently drops. What most likely happened?
options: Pagination parameters that select real content were stripped, collapsing threads onto page 1
The tracking-parameter list was too small, so campaign URLs still flooded the frontier queues
The canonicalizer uppercased percent-escapes, which made valid URLs fail to resolve
The seen-URL test began hashing raw URLs, so alias variants were fetched repeatedly

questions.question: A site labels every article's `rel="canonical"` link as its own homepage. How should an acquisition pipeline treat the canonical hint in general?
options: As a directive that must override the crawler's own URL normalization decisions
As a site-supplied hint to weigh against content-equality checks, never obeyed blindly
As a spam signal that should immediately exclude the entire host from the corpus
As a redirect equivalent, so the fetched URL is replaced by the declared canonical target
